I trust that this explanation of cheques Nos. 8399 and 8402, drawn against Trust Account No. 449, referred to in your
letter, will be satisfactory. Enclosed you will find our Inspectors report and a covering letter from Mr. Commissioner
Graham, both of which should be returned to this Department in, due course.

I am pleased to add, for your information, that I have known for some years of the unfortunate financial condition of
the Dunbow Industrial School. Once a large, prosperous institution, the pupillage dwindled until the per capita
earnings were unable to meet the current expense. For some considerable time the church workers in charge drew only
part salary, in an effort to keep the school in a solvent condition.


Yours very truly,
D.C. SCOTT, D.S.G.


The Assistant Auditor General.


AUDITOR GENERAL'S OFFICE, February 6, 1924.

SIR, - I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of January 3, last, enclosing Mr. Inspector Murison's report on the
closing of the Dunbow (St. Joseph's) Industrial School.

I wish to point out that, in my opinion, the procedure followed in closing this school was not, so far as financial
matters were concerned, in strict accordance with the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act. Mr.
Murison disposed of the effects of the school, either by sale or by distribu-



=== EXTRACT FROM HERE (pages 545-548) ===
<!-- page 545 -->
INDIAN AFFAIRS DEPARTMENT: CORRESPONDENCE

tion among other Indian schools; out of the proceeds of the sales he paid all outstanding accounts due by the school
with the exception of the arrears of salary due to the Principal and to the Grey Nuns. From the statements
accompanying Mr. Murison's report it appears that he collected in all $7,554.40 from which he paid out $1,527.61,
leaving a balance of $6,026.79 which was turned over to Commissioner Graham, who, intern, remitted it to your
department. Section 35 of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act provides that all public moneys, from whatever
source of revenue derived, shall be paid to the credit of the account of the Minister of Finance and Receiver General;
the term "public moneys" is fully defined in Section 2 (a) of the same act. In accordance with this provision the whole
amount collected by Mr. Murison should have been remitted to your department for deposit to the credit of the
Receiver General, and the outstanding accounts paid in the ordinary manner through your letter-of-credit. An advance
might have been made to Mr. Murison from your vote to provide for any small accounts that had to be paid on the
spot.

I notice that Mr. Murison's statement of payments made by him is not supported by any vouchers; he should be asked
to furnish detailed accounts with receipts for each item of his expenditure.

In the financial statement of the school for the period between April 1, and October 31, 1922, an item of $4,613.22 is
shown as having been paid out for salaries. Me statements of arrears of salaries show that the following amounts were
paid out during that period on account of salaries.

Principal, August 31 $500 00 ...
Sept. 18             600 00 ...
Oct. 31              1,000 00 ...
...                  ...      2,100 00
Grey Nuns, Oct. 17 ...        1,367 22
Total                ...      $3,467.22

I should like to know what salaries were included in the remaining amount of $1,146. I might add that Brother Thomas
Morkin, Farming Instructor, and Brother John Morkin, Engineer and Carpenter, were each paid $440 by Mr. Murison
on November 24, which is evidently 8 months' salary to November 30, at $55 a month.

I return Mr. Murison's report herewith.

I am, Sir, your obedient servant,
WM. KEARNS, Asst. A.G.

The Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs.

DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS, February 22, 1924.

SIR, - I have your letter of the 6th instant, with reference to the closing of the Dunbow (St. Joseph's) Indian
Residential School during the fiscal year 1922 - 23. I have noted that you consider the financial wind-up of this school
was not in strict accordance with the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act. I would point out that the
Church Authorities receive a per capita grant for their management and that they from time to time supplement the
parliamentary appropriation for both capital and current expenses at a government-owned Indian residential school.
Under these circumstances, are the moneys and movable assets public moneys and property?

<!-- page 546 -->
It was considered that the bank account, crop, stock, food and clothing and all equipment belonged to the State and the
Church jointly. Inspector Murison, in the case of the Dunbow Indian Residential School, was directed to assist the
Church Authorities in the closing so that our equity in movable assets would be safeguarded. Our officer was
instructed to co-operate with the Rev. Principal and to see that all bills were paid. Any equipment of value to the other
Indian residential schools managed by the same Order in the vicinity was distributed gratis. The remainder of the
movable assets were sold and the school bills including salary arrears having been paid, the balance, $477.42, was
deposited to Casual Revenue.

When Mr. Murison was paying the outstanding accounts, be telegraphed for permission to pay the arrears of salary. It
developed later that these amounted to $5,549.37. The Provincial of the Oblate Order at an earlier date had requested a
total cash consideration of $16,559.95 for their equity in the property. In view of these facts I consider it advisable,
before paying the arrears of salaries, to have Mr. Murison's audit and report before me. I therefore directed that the
funds concerning which you have raised questions be deposited in a special account.

Yours very truly,
D.C. SCOTT, D.S.G.

The Assistant Auditor General.

Civil Service Commission: Rate of Pay for Position of Inspector of Construction

AUDITOR GENERAL'S OFFICE, October 4, 1924.

SIR, - I beg to refer you to my letter of December 21st, 1923, with regard to the rates of compensation given in the
classification schedule for the position of Inspector of Construction and to your answer thereto of December 27th,
1923.

In your reply you state that my understanding of the matter coincides with that of the Commissioners, viz., that a man
appointed to a position in this class at a daily rate is entitled to pay only for those days on Which he is actually
engaged. on inspection work.

There is still a point in connection with the rates of compensation for this class on which I should like the opinion of
the Commission.

The monthly rate of salaries for this position ranges from $100 to $140, while the daily rate may be anything up to $7.
Am I to differ from this that an inspector employed at a daily rate of $6 or $7 a day, if employed more or less
continuously, may be paid up to $180 or $210 a month or will the amount of pay that he may receive during any
month be limited in any way by the prescribed monthly rates.

I am, sir, your obedient servant,
WM. KEARNS, Asst. A.G.

The Secretary, Civil Service Commission.

NOTE. - No reply had been received to the above letter up to the time of printing.

Unsatisfactory Certificates on Vouchers for Payments

AUDITOR GENERAL'S OFFICE, June 20, 1924.

SIR, - Trust Fund Cheque No. 5315, charged against the trust funds of the Mississaguas of the Credit, is for the
payment of $175 to Harvey Clark for pointing up and plastering the abutments under Boston Creek bridge. The
account is certified in the prescribed manner by the local Indian agent, it also bears some pencilled initials, presumably
those of some officer in your department but whose. initials they are I am unable to determine.

Section 55 of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act provides that "The deputy heads of the several departments or
the officers, clerks or other persons charged with the expenditure of public moneys, shall respectively audit the details.
of the accounts of the several services in the first instant, and be responsible for the correctness, of such audit". To
comply with this section, each paid account should bear a definite certificate that it has been examined by the proper
departmental officer or officers and found correct; all such certificates should be signed, not merely initialled, by the
examining officers.

I am, Sir, your obedient servant,
WM. KEARNS, Asst. A.G.

The Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs.

Indian Annuities: Unexpended Balance of Advance not Refunded by Agent

AUDITOR GENERAL'S OFFICE, September 20, 1924.

Sir, - Annuities Cheque No. 1487, issued on June 22, 1923, is for the payment of $850 to Mr. W.H. Lewis, Indian
Agent at the Timiskaming Agency, to enable him to pay annuities to the Abitibi Band of Indians.

According to the pay-sheets submitted by Mr. Lewis, The distributed $752 among the Indians leaving an unexpended
balance of $98. I find no trace of this balance having been refunded, and inquiry at your accountant's office reveals the
fact that this amount is still outstanding, although Mr. Lewis has accounted in full for the annuity advance for the
current fiscal year.

Kindly inform me what steps, if any, have been taken to recover this amount from Mr. Lewis.

I am, sir, your obedient servant,
WM. KEARNS, Asst. A.G.

The Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs.

DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS, September 24, 1924.

SIR, - In reply to your enquiry of the 20th instant, regarding $98, balance of undistributed annuity money which has
not been refunded by Mr. W.H. Lewis, Indian Agent, North Timiskaming, I beg to say that this Department has twice
brought this matter to the Agent's attention. He was informed recently that if he fails to make prompt refund, payment
of his salary will be withheld in order that the matter may be adjusted. If refund is not made by the end of the present
month the amount will be charged to his salary.

Your obedient servant,
J.D. MCLEAN, Act. D.S.G.

The Auditor General.

<!-- page 548 -->
Vote 274, Indians of Ontario and Quebec: Overpayment of Salary to Indian Agent J.R. McGregor


AUDITOR GENERAL'S OFFICE, February 5, 1924.

SIR, - On December 24th last, an Order in Council (P.C. 60/2521) was passed, based on a report from the Civil
Service Commission, granting permanent status from April 1st, 1923, to a number of employees of the Department of
Indian Affairs.

Among the employees so blanketed in I find the name of J.R. McGregor, Indian agent, grade 4, at Gore Bay, Ontario.
Mr. McGregor was first employed as agent on July 4th, 1916, at a salary of $800, and continued to be valid at that rate
until the reclassification, when, the position being classified as Indian Agent, grade 4, his salary was raised from
April 1st, 1919, to $1,440, the minimum of the class. Mr. McGregor's salary remained at $1,440 until April 1, 1922,
when it was raised to $1,560 (the next step) under the authority of a certificate issued by the Civil Service Commission
on May 11th, 1922, and a further increase to $1,680 was made on April 1st, 1923, under the authority of a certificate
issued on February 21st, 1923.

I beg to point out that in my opinion, if Mr. McGregor was considered a temporary employee only, until the passing of
the Order in Council of December 24th, 1923, he was not legally entitled to receive the increases granted on April 1st,
1922, and on April 1st, 1923, and that, accordingly, his permanent appointment should be only at the salary to which
he was legally entitled, viz., $1,440.


I am, sir, your obedient servant,
WM. KEARNS, Asst. A.G.

The Secretary, Civil Service Commission.
CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION, February 11, 1924.

SIR, - I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 5th instant with reference to the case of Mr. J.R. McGregor,
Indian Agent, Grade 4, at Gore Bay, Ont. The salary increases effective 1st April, 1922, and 1st April, 1923, to which
reference is made in your letter, were approved by the Civil Service Commission on the understanding that
Mr. McGregor was a permanent employee within the meaning of the definition of a permanent employee given by the
Department of Justice, the Department of Indian Affairs having informed the Commission that all the Indian Agents
had been regularly appointed to permanent positions by competent authority.

It was only after the salary increases had been approved that Mr. McGregor's temporary status was learned through the
recommendation of the Department that he be made permanent under the provisions of P.C. 2958. As Mr. McGregor
can only be considered as a temporary employee up to the date when he was made permanent under the blanketing
regulations, I am inclined to agree with you that the salary increases granted on the 1st April, 1922, and 1st April,
1923, were not legally authorized by the terms of the Civil Service Act and that Mr. McGregor was only entitled
therefore to receive on permanent appointment a salary rate, of $1,440 per annum.


I am, sir, your obedient servant,
WM. FORAN, Secretary.


The Assistant Auditor General.
